```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

Age is commonly expressed in whole numbers. For example, we might describe a person as 20 years old, while an infant's
age is more often expressed in months or weeks. More generally, age represents the elapsed time between a starting
point, such as birth, and a particular event. That event might be the onset of puberty, graduation from high school, a
first office visit, or the onset of an illness.

Age is an important characteristic in many types of analysis. Although we often work with individual ages, we also
frequently organize them into defined intervals or groups to summarize data, compare populations, and examine patterns
across different stages of life.

The agecraft package provides four S3 classes for representing ages and organizing them for analysis:

- age — Represents individual ages, expressed in units such as years, months, weeks, or days.
- age_interval — Represents a collection of defined age intervals used to classify observations. Each interval specifies 
a range of ages, and together the intervals establish the boundaries used to organize ages into groups.
- age_scheme — Contains an age_interval together with information about their source, provenance, and 
intended use. This allows established age-grouping schemes to be documented, shared, and applied consistently across 
analyses.
- age_group — Represents the classified age groups assigned to observations after their ages have been placed into the 
defined intervals. The resulting values identify the age group to which each observation belongs.

Together, these classes provide a structured approach to working with ages, from representing individual observations 
and defining age intervals to classifying ages and applying documented age-grouping schemes. 


## Observations to follow through the classes

The following fictional visit records include two infants, a child
exactly five years old, an adult, and a missing birth date. Each row is
one visit. 

```{r sample-data}
visits <- data.frame(
  id = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  birth_date = as.Date(c("2025-06-20", "2025-01-01", "2020-07-01",
                         "1980-01-01", NA)),
  visit_date = rep(as.Date("2025-07-01"), 5)
)
visits
```

## The age class: values with a unit

An `age` vector has the numeric ages with fractional precision and a time unit attached. Each element represents an age
value; the entire vector shares one unit, such as year, week, or day. Values in the vector are non-negative; missing
values are allowed and denoted with the usual R `<NA>`.

```{r calculate-ages}
# add ages to the data frame
visits$age <- calculate_age(visits$birth_date, visits$visit_date, unit = "year")
visits[c("id", "age")]
is_age(visits$age)

```


### Stored values and printed ages

The default display expresses ages as completed whole units, much as people
ordinarily report their age. Both infants therefore print as zero years,
although their stored ages differ. You can display those fractions or extract
the values explicitly:

```{r inspect-ages}
# Default display: completed whole units.  
# Note that the class name `age`,  unit 'year', and the length  are shown above the values.
visits$age

# Display fractional values without changing the age vector.
format(visits$age, fractional = TRUE)

# Extract completed-age character labels for reporting.
as.character(visits$age)

# Extract full numeric values, including fractions.
as.numeric(visits$age)

# Extract completed whole units as integers.
as.integer(visits$age)
```

`format()` returns a character representation while leaving the original object
unchanged. `as.character()` uses the same display rules: completed units by
default, or fractions with `fractional = TRUE`. Character labels preserve names
and missing values but carry no unit metadata. `as.numeric()` returns the full
stored values as an ordinary numeric
vector; `as.integer()` returns completed whole units as integers. Both extraction
methods remove the age class and its unit information.

For fractional display throughout a session, set
`options(agecraft.display.fractional = TRUE)`. This affects `format()`,
`as.character()`, ordinary printing, and tibble display. The default is `FALSE`;
an explicit `fractional` argument takes precedence. Stored values and group
assignments are unaffected.

The stored fractions allow classification within a whole unit. Two infants who
both print as zero years can still belong to different age groups. For example,
you might distinguish ages below 28 days from ages beginning at 28 days. For an
exact 28-day boundary, calculate ages and define the groups in days: a fraction
of a calendar year does not correspond to the same number of days for every
birth date.

#### Calendar anniversaries and elapsed time

`calculate_age()` returns `NA` and warns once with the affected count when an
end precedes its start. Other valid date pairs are still calculated; missing
date pairs remain missing without warning. Set
`options(agecraft.end_before_start = "error")` to stop on reversed dates during
a validation session, or `"warn"` for the default behavior.

When calculating an age from dates, the chosen unit determines how the
calculation works. Years and months follow calendar anniversaries, such as
birthdays or the same day in successive months. Their lengths vary: a year can
contain 365 or 366 days, and a month can contain 28 to 31 days. Weeks, days,
hours, minutes, and seconds have fixed relationships and can each be expressed
as a known number of seconds. Agecraft therefore calculates years and months
using calendar anniversaries and smaller units using elapsed time.

For years, `calculate_age()` counts completed birthdays and adds the fraction
of calendar days completed between the previous birthday and the next. For
months, it counts completed monthly anniversaries and adds the corresponding
fraction between consecutive anniversaries. These rules account for dates that
do not occur in every year or month:

- **Leap birthdays:** For someone born on February 29, the yearly anniversary
  falls on February 29 in a leap year and on March 1 by default in a non-leap
  year. Someone born on February 29, 2020 completes one year on March 1, 2021
  by default, or on February 28, 2021 with `leap_day = "feb28"`.
- **Month ends:** If the original day does not exist in the target month,
  the monthly anniversary falls on that month's last day. For someone born
  on January 31, 2025, the first two monthly anniversaries are February 28
  and March 31. Each anniversary is calculated from the original birth date,
  so the February adjustment does not move later anniversaries to the 28th.

For `POSIXct` date-times, calendar years and months use local dates in the
starting date-time's time zone. The end is interpreted in that same time zone,
and time of day is ignored. Someone born at 15:00 therefore completes a calendar
year on their anniversary date even when the reference time that day is before
15:00.

Elapsed time measures the duration between the two points, including their
times of day. This is useful when deciding, for example, whether a newborn is
less than 48 hours old. An elapsed day is exactly 24 hours, and an elapsed week
is seven such days. Consecutive local midnights can nevertheless be 23 or 25
hours apart when clocks change for daylight saving, producing `23 / 24` or
`25 / 24` elapsed days. Choose years or months for anniversary-based ages, and
smaller units when the elapsed duration matters.

### Constructing and using age values

If ages are already available as numbers, give them their known unit:

```{r construct-age}
known_ages <- age(c(0.5, 5, 45), unit = "year")
known_ages
```

Subsetting, sorting, and supported summaries retain the age class and
unit. Numeric addition and subtraction use that unit: `known_ages + 1`
adds one year. Negative results are rejected. Constructing an age from a
completed-year number cannot recover fractions that were discarded
earlier.

```{r subsetting-age}

# subset the first three.  The class 'age' is retained
visits$age[1:3]

# Many math and statistical functions can be used with an age vector.
mean(visits$age, na.rm = TRUE)
range(visits$age, na.rm = TRUE)

```


Use `as_age()` for explicit unit conversion. Days convert to weeks by a
fixed ratio. Conversions involving calendar months or years require
`allow_approx = TRUE`, including month-to-year conversion. When exact day-based
classification matters, calculate ages in days directly from those
dates.

## The age_interval class: ranges with boundaries

An age_interval vector represents age ranges that can be used to group observed ages. You can use it to define reporting
categories or describe an uncertain age when only a range is known. Each element has a lower and an upper bound. All
intervals are **left-closed and right-open**: they include the lower bound but exclude the upper bound. An age belongs
to an interval when:

`lower bound <= age < upper bound`

Mathematically, this is written as [lower, upper). The square bracket means “include this endpoint,” and the parenthesis
means “exclude this endpoint.”  This is the common understanding  of how we treat age groups.  

For example, the reporting category 1–4 years is represented by [1, 5). It includes ages from the first birthday up to, but not including, the fifth birthday. Ages 1, 3.5, and 4.9 belong to this interval; age 5 does not.

The vector also carries an optional time unit, optional interval names, and settings for displaying interval labels.
The ability to name an interval can be useful when you want to be more descriptive than just showing the ages.  For
example, the 0-1 year interval could be named `infant`.

For our visit records, define three illustrative reporting bands:

```{r define-intervals}
bands <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 1, 5, Inf), unit = "year")
names(bands) <- c("infant", "1 to under 5", "5 and older")
bands

data.frame(
  label = names(bands),
  lower = ivs::iv_start(bands),
  upper = ivs::iv_end(bands)
)
```

An interval includes its lower bound and excludes its upper bound: `[1, 5)` includes the first birthday and stops just
before the fifth. Its completed-age display is `1-4`. Exactly five belongs to `[5, Inf)`. Fractional bounds are
preserved; only upper bounds may be infinite. A missing interval has both bounds missing.

### Definitions exist independently of observations

There are three intervals here regardless of how many visit records we have. Naming a range makes its meaning readable
without changing its boundaries. Names do not change interval equality or chronological ordering.

```{r select-intervals}
bands[1:2]
compare_age_intervals(bands[1:2], operation = "width")
```

Widths use the interval's coordinate unit, years here. A width in years is not an exact elapsed-day duration since a
year can have 365 or 366 days. Selection and supported concatenation retain names and units; set operations may
merge or split intervals and therefore discard names.

An interval vector may have gaps or overlaps. Its class alone does not promise that every age belongs to exactly one
range. A unit of `NULL` means the unit is unspecified. For this guide, both the visit observations and the interval
definitions explicitly use years so their time units are directly comparable.

## The age_group class: assignments with their definitions

We have age observations and interval/group definitions. Classifying the
observations connects them:

```{r assign-groups}
visits$group <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = bands)
visits[c("id", "age", "group")]
class(visits$group)
table(visits$group, useNA = "ifany")
```

The result is an `age_group`, with classes `age_group`, `ordered`, and
`factor`. Each element is one observation's category assignment. Both
infants belong to "Under 1"; the child exactly five belongs to "5 and
older". The missing birth date produces a missing age and assignment. An
age outside every interval would also receive `<NA>`.  So, `<NA>` can be caused by a `<NA>` age   or when an age
not  covered by one of the defined intervals.

### What an assignment retains

Like an ordered factor, an `age_group` contains integer category codes and readable levels. It also retains one interval
definition per level, available through `group_intervals()`:

```{r inspect-groups}
levels(visits$group)
as.integer(visits$group)
group_intervals(visits$group)
```

The codes identify categories; they are not ages. The age_interval definitions have three elements, while the
ages-assignment vector has five, one per visit. Category levels follow interval order. The original exact ages and
scheme provenance are not stored in an `age_group`. Keep the age column when later calculations or new boundaries may
require it.

Subsetting preserves unused categories and their definitions. Remove them explicitly when a reduced set is wanted:

```{r subset-groups}
infants <- visits$group[1:2]
levels(infants)
levels(droplevels(infants))
```

Combining assignments requires matching ordered bounds, labels, and
definition units. Matching label text alone is insufficient. Use
`vctrs::vec_rbind()` when binding data frames containing these objects;
base data-frame binding can reconstruct factors and discard their
definitions. To obtain an ordinary factor, use `generics::as.factor()`
or `generics::as.ordered()` explicitly.

If you need a matched interval for each observation instead, request
interval output:

```{r matched-intervals}
matched <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = bands, output = "interval")
matched
length(matched)
```

This is an `age_interval` vector with one element per visit, including
repeated and missing intervals. It represents the matched ranges rather
than factor codes with a shared level definition.

## The age_scheme class: a reusable definition with context

Age groups are analytical choices. Their boundaries determine which
age-related differences remain visible and which are combined into a
single summary. A useful scheme preserves distinctions relevant to the
analysis question, supports reliable estimates, and permits the intended comparisons.
Published boundaries need to be assessed against the available observations
and population denominators.

An `age_scheme` brings interval definitions together with their origin and
intended use. Provenance records the source and history, including versions
and adaptations. Purpose and rationale explain what the scheme is intended
to describe and why the boundaries were chosen. For a worked comparison
showing how pooling can conceal infant incidence, see
[Choosing age groups for an analysis](v06-age_scheme_selection.html).
Here we follow how the class represents and retains those decisions.

```{r define-scheme}
visit_scheme <- age_scheme(
  intervals = bands,
  id = "example_visit_bands",
  name = "Illustrative visit reporting bands",
  type = "partition",
  domain = c(0, Inf),
  purpose = "Demonstrate age classes using fictional visits"
)
visit_scheme
scheme_intervals(visit_scheme)
```

This object contains the named `age_interval` vector. It also contains
its ID, name, purpose, partition/classification type, optional explicit domain,
calculated completeness, and provenance fields such as source, reference,
organization, version, and verification status. Information that is
unknown can remain unspecified. The scheme does not contain the visit
records or their assignments.

A scheme *contains* an age_interval vector.
Its intervals supply boundaries, labels, and units, while the scheme
supplies context and rules. The `scheme_intervals()` function retrieves the
definitions, and `summary()` reports coverage and provenance.

### Locate the definition, purpose, and source

The fictional visit scheme above has no external authority. To see how
source information accompanies published boundaries, use the childhood
pattern described in CDC's archived epidemiology teaching guidance. This
is a disease-surveillance pattern.

```{r sourced-childhood-scheme}
childhood_intervals <- age_interval(
  breaks = c(0, 1, 5, 10, 15, 20, Inf), unit = "year"
)
names(childhood_intervals) <- c("Under 1", "1-4", "5-9", "10-14", "15-19", "20+")
childhood_scheme <- age_scheme(
  childhood_intervals,
  id = "cdc_childhood_teaching", name = "CDC childhood teaching pattern",
  domain = c(0, Inf),
  purpose = "Retain infant and childhood detail for a teaching analysis",
  organization = "Centers for Disease Control and Prevention",
  source = "Principles of Epidemiology, Lesson 5, Section 5 (archived)",
  reference = paste0("https://archive.cdc.gov/www_cdc_gov/csels/dsepd/",
                     "ss1978/lesson5/section5.html"),
  verified = FALSE,
  notes = "Historical teaching guidance; source edition not recorded."
)
as.data.frame(childhood_scheme)
childhood_scheme$purpose
childhood_scheme$reference
```

Each data-frame row describes one interval. Its `start` and `end` columns are in the reported `unit`; the final `Inf`
denotes the top open-ended group. The `scheme_metadata` attribute carries the scheme's remaining metadata. For routine
interval operations such as categorizing ages, use the `scheme_intervals()` function to retrive the age_interval vector.

| Concept | Supported representation or inspection |
| --- | --- |
| Bounds, endpoint rule, labels, units | `scheme_intervals(x)` gives named, left-closed, right-open intervals; `as.data.frame(x)` displays bounds and units. |
| Source and edition | `x$organization`, `x$source`, `x$reference`, and `x$version`; unknown information can remain `NULL`. |
| Intended use and rationale | `x$purpose` and `x$notes`; there is no separate rationale or adaptation field. |
| Domain and completeness | `x$domain` stores NULL for inference or explicit bounds; `summary(x)` reports effective bounds, `domain_inferred`, gaps and calculated completeness. |
| Verification and ancestry | `x$verified` records the caller's claim; `x$derived_from` records ancestry after a tracked substantive edit. |
| Assigned observations | `categorize_age(ages, by = x)` returns an `age_group`; retain `x` separately for its provenance. |

This example leaves the source edition unspecified and verification false.
Attribution alone does not certify that the pattern suits a new question.
A scheme does not store population denominators, assess statistical precision,
or establish comparability with another report. Record those decisions with
the analysis. Use `notes` to explain a deliberate adaptation, and consult the
[schemes guide](v07-age-schemes.html) before editing a sourced definition.

### Validation expresses the intended classification

A `partition` prohibits overlapping categories. Completeness is calculated
against the inferred interval span or an explicit `domain`, independently of
overlap. With `domain = c(0, Inf)`, `summary(scheme)$complete` reports whether all
ages are covered. Without an explicit domain, `domain_inferred` in the summary
is TRUE; coverage outside the interval span cannot be assessed. A
`classification` may permit overlapping memberships and still be complete.

These checks establish properties of the definition. They do not
establish that its categories are appropriate for a reporting system or
independently verify an external source.

```{r use-scheme}
from_scheme <- categorize_age(visits$age, by = visit_scheme)
identical(from_scheme, visits$group)
```

Using this scheme produces the same assignments as its interval vector.
The assignments retain category definitions, while the scheme's identity
and provenance remain with the separate scheme object. Save the scheme
alongside the analysis when that context matters. Ordinary substantive
edits to a scheme are validated and track derivative ancestry; see the
schemes guide for details.

By default, `categorize_age()` rejects multiple matches. If a scheme
intentionally overlaps, `classify_age_scheme()` provides a table of all
memberships. Such a table is an ordinary data frame; overlapping
memberships cannot be summed as mutually exclusive population groups.

## Choosing what to retain

In the visit example, the dates allow recalculation, the `age` column
preserves precise values with units, and the `age_group` column supports
category tables while keeping the category bounds retrievable. The
separate `age_scheme` records the reusable definition and its context.

| Your next task | Object to retain |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------|
| Calculate or compare individual ages | Original dates and an `age` vector |
| Inspect or compare age ranges | An `age_interval` vector |
| Tabulate assigned categories and retrieve their bounds | An `age_group` vector |
| Reuse or document a classification definition | An `age_scheme` object |

Other familiar R classes appear at the boundaries: `Date` and `POSIXct`
supply dates and times; `units` vectors carry time quantities; ordinary
factors carry labels; and data frames hold observations or membership
tables. A scheme summary uses the supporting `summary_age_scheme` class
for readable printing. These support the four roles above without
replacing them.

For detailed assignment operations, see [Working with assigned age groups](v05-age-groups.html). For overlapping classifications,
provenance, and editing definitions, see [Creating and using reusable age schemes](v07-age-schemes.html). For individual arithmetic tasks, see [Calculating, comparing, and grouping ages](v04-age_math_examples.html). The
help topics `?age`, `?age_interval`, `?age_group`, and `?age_scheme`
provide their full construction and behavior contracts.
